extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of early-18th-century periodical essays; literate public interested in social criticism and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, satirical or moralizing periodical essays/letters (Spectator-style) that use character sketches, allegory, dream-visions, and social anecdote to instruct or amuse a general literate audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-specific inclinations and objects of desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Those ancients who considered the various bent and scope of our actions throughout the progress of life allotted inclinations and objects of desire particular to every stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowances should be made for natural tendencies at different life stages: indulge the levity of childhood with tenderness, overlook the gaiety of youth with good-nature, temper forward ambition of manhood with discretion, and impute tenacious avarice of old men to their want of relish for other enjoyment. This preserves decency and regularity in the course of life; inversion of these orders makes human nature appear ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decency and regularity (avoid inversion of social order)
rubrics_metrics.description: By maintaining a decency and regularity in the course of life, the dignity of human nature is supported; it suffers greatest violence when the order of things is inverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present feebleness attempting to adopt outward pomp and lustre appropriate to youth; such preposterous attempts are particularly vilifying and ridiculous. In narrative or social critique, preserve the appropriate relation between age, behaviour, and appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate parental provisioning and allowance for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: The skill should be to let a son want no lawful diversion, in proportion to his future fortune, and the figure he is to make in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing reasonable means and amusements prevents youths of quality from turning to cheats or debauchery out of want. The anti-pattern: fathers who deny necessary education or suitable allowances from affectation or narrow vanity, which produces social ills in offspring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the primary quality of a leader
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the first quality in the man who is in a post of direction; a just leader becomes beloved and honoured even without shining endowments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices demonstrating justice: keep dates of commissions, dismiss those deficient in duty, prefer according to order of battle, recommend extraordinary merit for distinction at court, and avoid favouritism. Short business, clear enforcement of duty, and promotion by merit maintain order and public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer merit over parade or favoritism
rubrics_metrics.description: The evils among mankind arise from the wanton disposition of the favours of the powerful; modesty and virtue can prosper only by finding some whim of a great man to open a way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should not reward mere appearance (profound faces, spectacles, extravagant dress) or courtly affectations; instead, prefer honest service and real merit. Examples show imposture by affected costume can gain access, but true governance should resist such superficial criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cultivating fools and buffoons in positions of favour
rubrics_metrics.description: A ruler's delight in fools, buffoons, humourists, and coxcombs is unworthy and dangerous; rejoicing in the disgrace of human nature or in the exhibition of impertinents lowers public reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favourites who are publicly made sport of can lead the populace to mock established offices and symbols (vestments, caps, barefoot affectations). Recommendation: bestow honours on the humble, virtuous, and meek; preserve the sanctity of authority through example and life rather than comic exhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegory as a valued compositional mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the finest compositions among the ancients are in allegory; there is a demand for allegorical papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors aiming to revive or employ allegory may find strong public appetite; allegory can be an effective vehicle for moral instruction and satire in periodical essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time and place (dramatic/structural unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticks in the coffee-houses talk mightily of the unity of time and place; an author may attempt something like it in a piece's opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not rigidly prescribed, attention to unity of time/place (or at least a disciplined framing of a scene) is a recognized critical expectation among contemporary reviewers and can lend a piece formal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dream/fiction devices for satire and exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'abuse' (satirize) a subject effectively, the writer is sometimes obliged to have recourse to dream and fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame satirical points as dreams, visions, or fictional evocations to soften direct offence while still exposing follies; Honeycomb's dream-vision about women carrying goods instead of husbands exemplifies this device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct orthography and copy-editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Small orthographical mistakes should be rectified before publishing ('after having rectified some little Orthographical Mistakes...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to spelling and small textual corrections in letters and submissions to maintain credibility and readability in a periodical context.
